•  The knockout of G2 abolishes resistance (g2 = 0 %), and in every double mutant that carries g2 (g1 g2 and g2 g3) resistance is also 0 %.  
  → the g2 phenotype masks (= is epistatic to) the phenotypes of the other mutations, so G2 must be the gene that is highest (up-stream) in the pathway.  
  → an up-stream gene that controls the activity of others is most readily explained as a transcription-factor gene; therefore G2 is the transcription factor.

•  Single mutants g1 (75 %) and g3 (50 %) are only partially affected, but the double mutant g1 g3 drops almost to zero (10 %).  
  → each of these two genes can supply part of the same protective function; only when both are missing is resistance virtually lost.  
  → this “either-one-is-enough” pattern is the hallmark of gene redundancy, not pleiotropy (one gene affecting several traits) and not “shared promoter”.

•  In the g1 g3 double mutant the phenotype is not the same as either single; no real epistasis between G1 and G3 is evident, so whichever of them is said to be epistatic to the other is essentially arbitrary.  Among the listed options, only one combines the correct identification of G2 as the transcription factor and the redundant relationship of G1 and G3.

Therefore the only choice that fits the main features of the data is option D.

Answer: D
